name: Microsoft COCO (Common Objects in Context)
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation in natural scenes. The dataset contains photos of 91 object types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old, with objects labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Images depict complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick,
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using a novel pipeline that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with scene-based queries to gather non-iconic images containing contextual relationships. The dataset harvested images containing contextual relationships and non-iconic object views by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. For categories where enough images could not be found, single category searches were performed with explicit filtering to remove iconic images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A filtering stage was applied to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate images. Workers were shown grids of 128 candidate images and asked to remove invalid or iconic images. Instructions included examples of iconic and non-iconic images to guide workers. Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using duplicate detection, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across dataset splits.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages: (1) Category labeling: Workers indicated which object categories were present by dragging category icons onto instances in the image. Eight workers labeled each image, and a category was considered present if any worker indicated it. (2) Instance spotting: Workers placed crosses on all instances of specific categories (up to 10 instances per category). Each image was labeled by 8 workers. (3) Instance segmentation: Workers segmented each object instance using a modified interface from the OpenSurfaces project. All workers were required to complete a training task for each object category before being allowed to segment instances. The training task required workers to segment an object instance and could not be completed until their segmentation adequately matched ground truth. Each instance was segmented by a single worker. For images with more than 10 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single (possibly multi-part) segment.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Modified user interface from OpenSurfaces project for segmentation tasks.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation and indicate whether it matched the instance well. Each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators. If any annotator indicated the segmentation was bad, it was shown to 2 additional workers. Segmentations that didn't receive at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded and the corresponding instances added back to the pool of unsegmented objects. Work from workers who consistently produced poor segmentations was discarded entirely.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Category labeling: 8 workers per image. Instance spotting: 8 workers per image. Instance segmentation: 1 worker per instance. Segmentation verification: 3-5 workers per segmentation.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The MS COCO dataset is split into two roughly equal parts. The first half was released in 2014, containing 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The second half was planned for release in 2015, with cumulative totals of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories out of the full 91 categories. Some categories may be added in the cumulative 2015 release.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses only on 'thing' categories (objects for which individual instances may be easily labeled) and does not include 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The authors note that labeling 'stuff' categories could provide significant contextual information useful for detection. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories commonly used by humans when describing objects, and does not include fine-grained categories or object-part categories. Eleven categories were excluded from the 2014 release: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (confusion with bowl and dining table), and blender, hair brush (too few instances).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for object detection and segmentation tasks. It addresses three core research problems in scene understanding: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. The dataset can be used for training and evaluating object detection algorithms, instance segmentation algorithms, and scene understanding models. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test data. An evaluation server was planned for automatic evaluation on the test set.
